strengths: Addresses an underexplored but important axis of MDM inference—the unmasking order—rather than the more commonly studied denoiser training, and provides a compelling motivating experiment (Pass@N on GSM8K) showing that substantially better unmasking trajectories exist beyond max-confidence.

Provides non-trivial theoretical contributions: extends Mroueh's GRPO convergence analysis with a new 'Reference-KL Tightening' theorem showing the learned policy's terminal-output distribution is provably closer to the data distribution than a strong reference heuristic, under stated assumptions.

Careful bridging of theory to practice: derives tractable token-level surrogates (Proposition 1) and KL surrogates (Propositions 2-3) with rigorous appendix proofs adapted to the non-standard (sparse-reward, finite-horizon, non-stationary) MDP setting of MDM denoising.
Memory-efficient practical design that reuses frozen MDM features and trains a small policy head (134M vs 8B parameters), enabling single-GPU training—an appealing systems contribution.

Reasonably broad empirical validation across four diverse benchmarks (two logic puzzles, two math-reasoning tasks) with consistent improvement or parity versus multiple strong heuristic baselines (random, margin, entropy, confidence).
Useful ablations demonstrating compatibility with existing RL post-training (diffu-GRPO) and the practical value of the KL/CE regularization term for avoiding premature convergence.
weaknesses: Empirical gains are inconsistent in magnitude and in one case (MATH500) only tie rather than exceed the best heuristic baseline (margin), weakening the claim of consistently surpassing heuristics.

The strongest theoretical guarantee (Theorem 2) rests on idealized assumptions (existence of a perfect MDM θ* with zero loss, exact support containment between gref and θ*) that are unlikely to hold in the practical large-scale setting actually evaluated, creating a gap between the theory and the heuristic surrogate objective (LUPO) that is actually optimized.
Evaluation is limited to a single base MDM (LLaDA-8B-Instruct); no experiments on other MDMs (e.g., Dream-7B) to demonstrate generality of the approach.

The best-performing reference policy (gref) differs by task (max-confidence for logic puzzles, Top-K for math), with no principled a priori method for choosing it—this is acknowledged as future work but limits the practicality/generality of the framework as presented.

No direct quantitative comparison against the closest related method, DCOLT (Huang et al., 2025), beyond an internal ablation proxy ('random initialization'); a head-to-head comparison would better substantiate the claimed advantages.

No variance/error bars or multiple seeds reported for the main results (Table 2), making it hard to assess statistical significance of the reported gains, some of which are small (e.g., ZEBRA 33.7%→36.2%).
No discussion or measurement of the additional inference-time compute/latency overhead introduced by the policy model's extra transformer layer and MLP at every denoising step.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated problem: the unmasking order in MDMs is known to substantially affect generation quality, and moving beyond hand-crafted heuristics (max-confidence/margin) to a learned scheduler is a reasonable direction.
The Pass@N analysis on GSM8K (Figure 1) provides a clear empirical motivation that better-than-max-confidence unmasking trajectories exist, justifying the pursuit of a learned policy.

The memory-efficient training design (reusing frozen MDM features/Top-K logits as inputs to a small 134M-parameter policy head) is a practical engineering contribution that keeps training feasible on a single GPU for an 8B base model.
The ablation showing compatibility/composability with diffu-GRPO (post-training the base MDM) suggests the method can stack with existing RL fine-tuning approaches.

The paper attempts a fairly extensive theoretical treatment (regularized MDP formulation, convergence/KL-tightening theorems, surrogate objective derivations) which, if sound and tight, would be a differentiator from purely heuristic or purely empirical prior work (e.g., DCOLT).
weaknesses: Theorem 1 is merely a restatement of an existing result from Mroueh (2025) and is presented in a way that could mislead readers into thinking it is a novel contribution of this paper; the real "new" theorem (Theorem 2) critically depends on this borrowed, idealized tabular/distributional convergence result, whose assumptions (exact optimization over the full output distribution, no function approximation error, no sampling noise) do not hold in the actual neural, sampled, clipped implementation used in experiments.

Theorem 2 requires an unrealistic "ideal MDM" with zero loss and a support-inclusion assumption on the reference policy; these assumptions are essentially never satisfiable in practice for large-scale LLaDA-8B on hard reasoning tasks, so the theoretical guarantee that the learned policy is "closer to pdata" does not meaningfully transfer to the empirical setting, despite being advertised prominently in the abstract ("we prove that the optimized policy ... generates samples that more closely match the data distribution").

The gap between the theoretical objective (Eq. 10, intractable output-level GRPO with exact KL) and the practical training loss (Eq. 19, with token-level surrogate, clipping, and ad hoc divergence terms like cross-entropy to gconf that the authors themselves admit is "not theoretical") is large; Proposition 1 is only approximate ("informal", holds exactly only at the first gradient step), undermining the paper's central claim that the practical algorithm inherits the stated guarantees.

Empirical gains are inconsistent and in some cases marginal: on Zebra the improvement over the best heuristic is only ~0.6-2.5 points, and on MATH500 the method merely ties the strongest baseline (0.284 vs 0.284) rather than improving on it, weakening the claim of consistent superiority over heuristics.

No variance/error bars, confidence intervals, or multiple-seed results are reported for the main results (Table 2) or the diffu-GRPO compatibility result (Table 3), making it impossible to assess whether the reported gains (some under 1-2 points) are statistically meaningful versus noise.

DCOLT, explicitly called out as the closest related/competing method, is only compared in an ablation on two benchmarks (Figure 3) and not included as a baseline in the main results table (Table 2) across all four benchmarks, leaving an important comparison incomplete.

The best-performing reference policy realization (gref) differs by task (max-confidence for Sudoku/Zebra, Top-K for GSM8K/Math500) with no principled rule for selecting it a priori, which suggests the method requires per-task tuning/model selection and is less "general" than advertised; this also raises concerns about overfitting to each benchmark's validation behavior.

All experiments use a single base model (LLaDA-8B-Instruct); no results are shown on other MDMs (e.g., Dream-7B) to demonstrate that the learned policy and its theoretical framing generalize beyond one specific model/architecture.

The reward design differs across task types (dense partial-credit reward for logic puzzles vs. sparse 0/1 terminal reward for math) without a unified justification, and the theoretical analysis (e.g., Theorem 2) assumes binary verifiable rewards, creating an inconsistency between theory and the dense-reward logic-puzzle experiments.

The method requires white-box access to the frozen MDM's internal transformer features and token-probability outputs, making it architecturally coupled to the specific base model in a way that pure heuristic schedulers (max-confidence, margin) are not, somewhat limiting its plug-and-play applicability despite being framed as a drop-in replacement for heuristics.

strengths: Novel and practical framing: decoupling the unmasking order policy from the underlying MDM and training only a small policy head (134M params) with the base MDM frozen, enabling memory-efficient training (claimed single A100-40GB) while large-scale MDMs (e.g., LLaDA-8B) remain untouched.

Solid theoretical scaffolding: casts unmasking as a KL-regularized MDP, connects to GRPO convergence theory (Mroueh, 2025), and derives a novel KL-tightening theorem arguing the learned policy's terminal distribution is provably closer to the data distribution than the reference heuristic under stated assumptions.

Careful handling of intractability: provides rigorous (if lengthy) proofs adapting the policy gradient theorem to the sparse-reward, finite-horizon, non-stationary MDP setting specific to MDM denoising, and derives tractable token-level surrogate losses (including a KL surrogate and cross-entropy variant for deterministic references) with proofs of gradient equivalence.

Reasonably comprehensive empirical study: consistent improvements over random/margin/entropy/confidence heuristics on four diverse benchmarks (SUDOKU, ZEBRA, GSM8K, MATH500), plus a motivating Pass@N analysis showing headroom beyond max-confidence, and ablations on regularization strength and reference-policy choice.

Demonstrated orthogonality/compatibility with existing RL-based MDM post-training (diffu-GRPO), showing additive gains when combining both lines of work, which strengthens the practical relevance of the contribution.
weaknesses: Theorem 2's guarantee formally requires a reference policy gref with full support overlapping the ideal model's support, but in practice the strongest reference used for the main results (gconf, used for SUDOKU/ZEBRA) is deterministic and handled via an ad hoc cross-entropy surrogate explicitly outside the theoretical framework ("Although not theoretical..."), creating a gap between the theory and what is actually deployed in the best-performing configurations.

The idealized assumptions in Theorem 2 (existence of an ideal MDM with LMDM(θ*)=0, oracle reward, support containment) are strong and somewhat detached from the realistic setting of an imperfect pretrained MDM with limited verifiable rewards, limiting how much the theoretical result explains the empirical gains.

The main convergence result (Theorem 1) is a direct restatement of prior work (Mroueh, 2025) rather than a new contribution, and the genuinely novel theoretical content (Theorem 2, Propositions 1-3) is comparatively narrow in scope.

Evaluation is limited to a single base model (LLaDA-8B-Instruct) and four narrow benchmark types (two logic puzzles, two math datasets); no results on open-ended generation, code, or a second MDM backbone (e.g., Dream-7B) to assess generality.

The reference policy choice is tuned per-task (gconf for puzzles, Top-K for math) with no single policy/recipe that works uniformly well, and the paper itself flags this as unresolved future work, suggesting the method is not yet a drop-in general-purpose replacement for heuristic schedulers.

DCOLT (Huang et al., 2025), the most directly comparable prior work on learned unmasking policies, is only indirectly compared via a "random initialization" ablation in Section 4.2, not included as a baseline in the main results table (Table 2), making it hard to assess how much of the gain comes from the regularized-MDP formulation versus simply learning any policy.

Gains on MATH500 are marginal (tying with the margin baseline at 28.4%), and no variance/confidence intervals are reported across runs, making it hard to assess the statistical robustness of reported improvements.

The method adds considerable complexity (dedicated policy network, careful reference-policy-dependent loss design, pretraining/initialization schemes) which may hinder reproducibility and adoption despite the claimed memory efficiency.

strengths: Well-motivated problem: the paper identifies a genuine gap in MDM literature — reliance on heuristic unmasking schedules (max-confidence, max-margin) rather than learned policies — and provides empirical evidence (Pass@N analysis in Fig. 1) that better unmasking orders exist beyond max-confidence, motivating the approach.

Solid theoretical grounding: the paper casts unmasking-order selection as a KL-regularized MDP and provides two theorems (policy improvement convergence building on Mroueh 2025, and KL-tightening showing the learned policy's output distribution is provably closer to the data distribution than the reference policy), with detailed proofs in the appendix, including careful handling of the non-standard MDP structure (sparse terminal reward, finite horizon, state spaces per layer) via a custom policy gradient lemma.

Practical/tractable derivation: the paper carefully bridges the intractable output-level GRPO objective to a tractable token-level surrogate (Proposition 1) and a tractable KL surrogate (Propositions 2/3), with three different reference-policy realizations (max-confidence, softmax, Top-K), each justified and empirically compared.

Reasonably broad empirical validation across four benchmarks (SUDOKU, ZEBRA, GSM8K, MATH500) using a large-scale pretrained MDM (LLaDA-8B), with consistent improvements over multiple heuristic baselines (random, margin, entropy, confidence), plus a compatibility experiment showing gains stack on top of diffu-GRPO post-training.

Memory-efficient practical design: the policy model reuses frozen MDM features (adding only a lightweight transformer + MLP, ~134M params vs 8B base model), which is a nice systems-level contribution enabling training on a single GPU.

Useful ablations (regularization strength/variance analysis, binary vs dense reward, Pass@N of the learned policy, generalization to preference-based ARM-likelihood rewards) that partially address robustness and generalizability concerns.
weaknesses: Gains are inconsistent and sometimes marginal: on MATH500 the method merely ties the best baseline (28.4% vs margin's 28.4%) rather than surpassing it, and on GSM8K/MATH500 gains over max-confidence are modest (e.g., 70.3% vs 68.4%), undermining claims of consistent superiority; the paper's own discussion admits gains shrink outside SUDOKU without fully resolving why.

The best-performing reference-policy realization is task-dependent (max-confidence realization best for SUDOKU, Top-K best for GSM8K) with only post-hoc conjectures for why, suggesting the practical framework requires per-task tuning/realization choice rather than a single robust recipe, which weakens claims of a general solution.

Theoretical guarantees rely on strong/idealized assumptions (e.g., existence of an ideal MDM θ* with zero loss, well-defined binary reward aligned perfectly with pdata support, exact convergence of GRPO fixed-point dynamics from Mroueh 2025) that may not hold in the practical dense-reward, clipped, surrogate-loss setting actually used in experiments — the practical objective (Eq. 19, with clipping and token-level surrogate) is only approximately justified (Proposition 1 is 'informal' and only exact at ϕ=ϕold), leaving a gap between what is proven and what is run.

Baseline comparisons may be somewhat narrow: the primary comparisons are against simple decoding heuristics (random, margin, entropy, confidence) for the base model, but there is limited comparison against other learned-scheduler approaches beyond a same-paper reimplementation of DCOLT (as a randomly-initialized ablation) rather than the published DCOLT numbers/setup, making it hard to assess true competitiveness against the closest related learned-policy work (Huang et al. 2025).

Reward design for math benchmarks incorporates an auxiliary log-probability-based dense reward that is somewhat ad hoc (relative binning into discrete reward levels) and not theoretically justified, which is inconsistent with the paper's own theory (Theorem 2) that is stated specifically for binary rewards; the binary-reward experiments (Appendix D.1) are limited to two benchmarks and show smaller gains, suggesting the strong headline numbers partly rely on this extra engineering choice rather than the core theoretical mechanism.

Limited scale/generality of evaluation: experiments are restricted to one base model (LLaDA-8B-Instruct) and small/narrow benchmark types (logic puzzles and grade-school/competition math); the promising but very preliminary generalization experiment (Appendix D.2, ARM-likelihood reward) uses only two datasets and reports a single accuracy number without ablations, limiting confidence that findings generalize to broader open-ended NLG tasks.

The paper doesn't report computational overhead/inference latency introduced by the extra transformer+MLP scoring pass per denoising step, which is relevant for practical adoption given that unmasking-order search is itself argued to be a costly bottleneck.

Only single-run point-estimates are reported for main results (Table 2), without variance/confidence intervals across seeds, making it hard to assess whether some of the smaller reported gains (e.g., MATH500, GSM8K) are statistically meaningful.

strengths: Novel formulation of discrete-diffusion unmasking order selection as a KL-regularized MDP, with explicit theoretical guarantees (fixed-point convergence beyond the reference policy via Mroueh's GRPO dynamics, and a KL-tightening result showing the learned policy's terminal distribution is provably closer to the true data distribution than the reference).

Careful treatment of the output-level vs. token-level intractability gap: Proposition 1 (gradient alignment) and Propositions 2-3 (surrogate KL bound and its tractable gradient) give some justification for the practical PPO/GRPO-style loss used in training.
Thoughtful, memory-efficient implementation: a lightweight policy head (134M) riding on frozen MDM features (8B), with a detailed training algorithm (Algorithm 2) enabling single-GPU training.

Reasonably broad empirical validation across four benchmarks (SUDOKU, ZEBRA, GSM8K, MATH500), plus informative ablations: choice of reference policy, effect of the divergence regularizer on preventing premature convergence, binary vs. dense reward, and compatibility with diffu-GRPO (showing complementary gains when combined with MDM-level RL fine-tuning).

The Pass@N analysis (Fig. 1 and Fig. 8) gives a clear motivating argument that better-than-max-confidence orderings exist, and ties nicely to the Gumbel-softmax multi-shot extension of the learned policy.
weaknesses: Empirical gains are highly uneven and modest on the harder/more realistic benchmarks: the headline SUDOKU result (+11.2% over max-confidence) is the main selling point, but on ZEBRA the gain is marginal (33.7%->36.2%), and on MATH500 the method merely ties the best baseline (28.4% vs 28.4%) while only modestly beating max-confidence on GSM8K (68.4%->70.3%). This undercuts the generality claim of the method.

No single configuration works across tasks: the best reference policy (max-confidence vs Top-K) must be chosen per-task via trial, and the paper offers only a post-hoc conjecture (exploration/search-space size) rather than a principled or automatic selection rule, weakening the claim of a unified, general-purpose framework.

The theory-practice gap is significant: Theorem 1/2 assume exact optimization of the idealized output-level objective with a well-defined binary reward and full-support reference policy, whereas the actual algorithm optimizes a clipped, token-level, Monte-Carlo surrogate, uses dense/shaped rewards in most experiments, and the gradient-alignment proposition is only guaranteed to hold exactly at a single optimization step, with approximate equality elsewhere and no quantitative bound on the approximation error.

The approach requires a verifiable/oracle reward signal and per-task RL training of a separate policy network, limiting applicability to open-ended generation; the one preliminary attempt at a general reward (Qwen-3 log-likelihood, Appendix D.2) is thin (two datasets, a single downstream accuracy number, no human or automatic quality metrics) and feels like an afterthought rather than a validated contribution.

Baseline comparisons are limited to simple heuristic schedulers (random, margin, entropy, confidence) and one ablation resembling DCOLT; there is no comparison against other plausible learned-policy approaches or more thorough analysis of why the proposed KL-regularized scheme should be preferred to simpler RL baselines beyond the single random-init ablation.

Additional training/inference overhead (separate policy network, RL training per task, extra forward passes through a transformer+MLP head) is not clearly weighed against the modest accuracy gains on math benchmarks, raising questions about practical cost-benefit versus simply using max-confidence or Top-K sampling.

Presentation is dense and proof-heavy in the main text, with core practical details (e.g., why cross-entropy is used instead of KL for the deterministic gconf reference, reparameterization tricks) deferred to the appendix, making it hard to assess rigor without extensive cross-referencing.

strengths: The paper tackles a well-motivated and underexplored problem: learning the unmasking position-selection policy for masked diffusion models, rather than relying on heuristic schedulers like max-confidence or max-margin.

The theoretical framework is thorough and clearly connected to practice: the paper proves a GRPO-style convergence theorem (Theorem 1, building on Mroueh 2025) and a novel KL-tightening result (Theorem 2) showing the learned policy's terminal distribution is provably closer to the data distribution than a strong reference policy, under reasonable support assumptions.

The derivation from the intractable output-level objective to a tractable token-level surrogate (Proposition 1) and the tractable KL surrogate for the regularizer (Propositions 2-3) are carefully derived with full proofs in the appendix, bridging theory and a practical, memory-efficient algorithm (Algorithm 2) that trains a lightweight policy (134M) on top of a frozen 8B MDM using a single GPU.

Empirical results are consistent and plausible: the learned policy matches or beats random, margin, entropy, and confidence baselines across four diverse benchmarks (SUDOKU, ZEBRA, GSM8K, MATH500), with especially large gains on SUDOKU where unmasking order matters most.

Good set of ablations: training dynamics across different reference policies (Fig. 3), compatibility with diffu-GRPO (showing the method is complementary to MDM-level RL fine-tuning), power-of-regularization study showing the KL/CE term prevents premature convergence, and an additional experiment with binary vs. dense rewards confirming robustness to reward design choice.
The qualitative SUDOKU unmasking visualizations (Appendix F) provide intuitive, convincing illustrations of why learned ordering outperforms max-confidence.

The paper is transparent about limitations (smaller gains on GSM8K/MATH500) and offers plausible explanations and future directions, and includes a preliminary generalization experiment using ARM log-likelihood as reward on an out-of-domain benchmark (Natural Questions).
weaknesses: The gains on GSM8K and MATH500 are quite modest (e.g., MATH500 ties the best baseline rather than exceeding it), and the explanation for why math reasoning benefits less is largely conjectural without deeper analysis or additional controlled experiments.

The reference policy realization that works best differs by task (max-confidence for SUDOKU/ZEBRA, Top-K for GSM8K/MATH500), and the paper does not provide a principled way to select or predict which realization suits a new task a priori, reducing the practicality of the method for unseen settings.

Evaluation is limited to a single base model (LLaDA-8B-Instruct); it is unclear whether results generalize to other MDMs (e.g., Dream-7B) or to larger diffusion LMs, which weakens claims of general applicability.

The max-confidence realization abandons the theoretical KL-regularized framework in favor of an ad hoc cross-entropy regularizer (since gconf is deterministic and ill-posed for KL), which somewhat undercuts the paper's central theoretical narrative for exactly the setting where the method performs best (SUDOKU).

Benchmark sizes/difficulty are relatively narrow (4x4 Sudoku rather than full 9x9, simplified Zebra, standard GSM8K/MATH500); scalability to more complex structured reasoning tasks or longer sequences is not demonstrated.

No comparison against other learned-ordering approaches is thoroughly benchmarked except DCOLT (reduced to a random-initialization ablation); a more direct, full reproduction/comparison against DCOLT and other recent unmasking-policy learning baselines would strengthen the empirical claims.

Theorem 2's practical implications rely on an idealized MDM θ* with zero training loss, and the connecting logic to the actual frozen, imperfect MDM used in experiments is somewhat informal (discussed in the main text but not rigorously bridged in the finite-sample, imperfect-model regime).
